title: We keep having the same fight
blurb: For the argument that resolves and then returns, in a slightly different costume.
entry_signals: it starts about the dishes and ends somewhere else

steps.ask: How raw is it right now, one to ten?

steps.title: Later is better for this one
steps.say:
This flow asks you to be unflattering about your own motives, and that's close to impossible mid-conflict — under threat everyone argues for survival rather than accuracy.

Come back when it's cooled. The recurring fight will still be recurring.

steps.ask: In these fights, does anything happen that you'd be worried about if a friend described it?
steps.help: Contempt, threats, anything that leaves you managing their reaction rather than discussing the matter. Recurring conflict and an unsafe dynamic can look similar from inside and are not the same thing.

options.label: I'm not sure — it gets bad but I don't know if that's normal

steps.title: Start there instead
steps.say:
That's a different question from why an argument repeats, and it comes first.

A useful check: is your partner the person who knows the most about how you feel in this relationship, or do your friends know more? A large gap there says something about how much of it is survivable to say out loud.
cites: Confiding In Friends Not The Partner
Taking Your Partner At Face Value

steps.ask_a: What is the fight nominally about?
steps.help_a: The stated subject. Chores, messages, their friend, the plan for Saturday.
steps.ask_b: What does it always turn into?
steps.help_b: The place it reliably ends up, however it starts.

steps.ask: When it's going badly, what are you fighting to protect?
steps.help: Not what you're saying — what you'd be unwilling to lose. This is the uncomfortable question in the whole flow and the one that moves things.
cites: Asking What You Are Actually Arguing For

options.label: That they still want me. That we're okay
options.names: A Partner Will Make Me Feel Worthy
cites: A Partner Will Make Me Feel Worthy

options.label: My time, my autonomy, not being taken from
options.names: Depending On Others Costs Me Myself
cites: Depending On Others Costs Me Myself

options.label: Their picture of me as a good person
cites: A Relationship Is A Checklist Item

options.label: Being the one who decides how things go

steps.ask: And what do you think they're fighting to protect?
steps.help: Their want, not their attachment style — what they're trying to keep, in ordinary words. Guessing at their diagnosis is the fastest way to make this worse.
cites: Taking Your Partner At Face Value

steps.say: So the argument has two layers: the one being had out loud, and the one underneath it. When neither underneath-layer gets stated, the surface argument can be won repeatedly and resolve nothing — which is exactly what a fight that keeps coming back looks like.

steps.ask: How would you say your real one out loud?
steps.help: Say it plainly enough that it could be refused. "I want to know we're okay before I can talk about the dishes" is a sentence someone can respond to. It also risks them saying no, which is the part that makes it worth something.

steps.ask: When one of you gets it wrong, what usually happens next?

options.label: We repair — someone owns it and we come back
It goes quiet and we move on without addressing it
One of us apologises to end the discomfort, not because it's resolved

steps.say: The sentence you wrote at the end is the whole point of this one. A recurring fight usually recurs because the real premise has never been on the table where it could be agreed to or turned down.
